The '''2022 United States House of Representatives elections in New Mexico''' were held on November 8, 2022, to elect the three [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representatives]] from the [[U.S. state|state]] of [[New Mexico]], one from each of the state's three [[New Mexico's congressional districts|congressional districts]]. The elections coincided with the [[2022 New Mexico gubernatorial election|New Mexico gubernatorial election]] and various [[2022 New Mexico elections|state and local elections]]. The Democratic party gained the 2nd Congressional seat, gaining unitary control of New Mexico's Congressional (House and Senate) delegation for the first time since 2018 and improving the advantage in the House delegation for New Mexico from 2–1 in favor of Democrats to 3–0.

== Redistricting ==
=== Process ===
In New Mexico, legislative and congressional maps must be passed by the [[New Mexico Legislature|state legislature]] and are subject to a [[veto]] by the [[Governor of New Mexico|governor]], which would require a two-thirds [[supermajority]] in each house of the legislature to [[veto override|override]]. In April 2021, governor [[Michelle Lujan Grisham]] signed a bill passed by the legislature that established the seven-member New Mexico Citizen Redistricting Committee. The job of the committee is to draw three sets of legislative and congressional maps, which it then sends to the legislature for consideration. Current public officials and government employees are barred from serving on the committee. The committee's role is purely advisory and the legislature is free to alter or discard its proposals.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Redistricting in New Mexico after the 2020 census |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_New_Mexico_after_the_2020_census |website=Ballotpedia}}</ref>

On October 15, 2021, the redistricting committee voted to send 3 congressional maps to the legislature. The first would largely maintain the boundaries of the state's existing map. The second would increase Native American representation in the [[New Mexico's 3rd congressional district|3rd congressional district]] to nearly 20% and Hispanic representation in the [[New Mexico's 2nd congressional district|2nd district]] to 54%. This proposal was championed by the committee's chairman [[Edward L. Chávez|Edward Chávez]], former [[Chief Justice]] of the [[New Mexico Supreme Court]]. The third, drawn by the Center for Civic Policy, would add liberal areas of the city of [[Albuquerque]] to the rural 2nd district.<ref>{{Cite web |date=Oct 15, 2021 |title=Advisory panel endorses redistricting maps for New Mexico |url=https://apnews.com/article/new-mexico-race-and-ethnicity-legislature-voting-rights-redistricting-f63b3551236a6041928b75cd256e92bf |website=AP NEWS}}</ref>

=== Targeting of the 2nd district ===
In the leadup to the [[2020 United States redistricting cycle|2020 redistricting cycle]], some suspected that the Democratic-controlled state legislature might alter the boundaries of the [[New Mexico's 2nd congressional district|2nd congressional district]] to make it more favorable to the Democratic Party. The 2nd district was represented by Democrat [[Xochitl Torres Small]] after she defeated Republican [[Yvette Herrell]] in the [[2018 United States House of Representatives elections in New Mexico#District 2|2018 midterm elections]], but she lost to Herrell in a [[2020 United States House of Representatives elections in New Mexico#District 2|2020 rematch]]. The day after Herrell's victory, Democrat [[Brian Egolf]], the [[Speaker of the New Mexico House of Representatives]], pointed out that the 2nd district would inevitably be changed during redistricting and said "we'll have to see what that means for Republican chances to hold it." This statement was criticized by [[Steve Pearce (politician)|Steve Pearce]], the chair of the [[New Mexico Republican Party]], who called it "political tricks."<ref name="plan">{{Cite web |last=Bryan |first=Susan Montoya |title=New Mexico Dems plan to redraw 2nd Congressional district |url=https://www.lcsun-news.com/story/news/politics/2020/11/05/democrats-nm-plan-redraw-2nd-congressional-district/6181346002/ |website=Las Cruces Sun-News}}</ref>

The district is mostly rural and dominated by the [[oil and natural gas industry]]. [[Carlsbad, New Mexico|Carlsbad]] mayor Dale Janway expressed concern that portions of the [[Albuquerque]] suburbs might be added to the district, which would dilute the influence of the rural communities in the district, including Carlsbad.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Janway |first=Dale |title=City of Carlsbad: Understanding the redistricting process |url=https://www.currentargus.com/story/opinion/columnists/2021/09/20/understanding-redistricting-process/8419391002/ |website=Carlsbad Current-Argus}}</ref> After the 2020 elections, the district held a [[Partisan Voting Index]] of R+8.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Introducing the 2021 Cook Political Report Partisan Voter Index |url=https://www.cookpolitical.com/analysis/national/pvi/introducing-2021-cook-political-report-partisan-voter-index |website=Cook Political Report|date=April 15, 2021 }}</ref>

=== Legislature's map ===
On December 10, the [[New Mexico Senate]] voted 25–15 to approve a congressional map drawn by Democratic state senator [[Joseph Cervantes]]. This proposal largely resembles the third map submitted by the commission, adding portions of western and southern [[Albuquerque]] to the [[New Mexico's 2nd congressional district|2nd district]] and moving a portion of the conservative-leaning, oil-producing area of the 2nd district into the [[New Mexico's 3rd congressional district|3rd district]]. These changes would increase the Hispanic majority in the 2nd district from 51% to 56% and decrease the percentage of Native Americans in the 3rd district from 20% to 16%. Republicans widely opposed the map, with GOP state senator [[David Gallegos]] pointing out that the map combines the conservative [[oilfield]] town of [[Hobbs, New Mexico|Hobbs]] with heavily Democratic [[Santa Fe, New Mexico|Santa Fe]], which is hundreds of miles away, and GOP senator [[Cliff Pirtle]] claiming that the map represented an attempt by Democrats to control all 3 of New Mexico's House seats. The 1st district covers the center of the state, taking in the counties of [[Torrance County, New Mexico|Torrance]], [[Guadalupe County, New Mexico|Guadalupe]], [[De Baca County, New Mexico|De Baca]], and [[Lincoln County, New Mexico|Lincoln]], as well as eastern [[Bernalillo County, New Mexico|Bernalillo County]] and most of [[Albuquerque, New Mexico|Albuquerque]].<ref name="2023map">{{cite web |title=Redistricting Maps and Data - Final Version |work=New Mexico Legislature |date=December 10, 2021 |access-date=May 3, 2022 |url=https://www.nmlegis.gov/Redistricting2021/Maps_And_Data?ID202=221711.1}}</ref> Democrat [[Deb Haaland]], who was re-elected with 58.2% of the vote in 2020,<ref name="clerk2020">{{cite web|last=Johnson|first=Cheryl L.|title=Statistics of the Congressional Election of November 3, 2020|url=http://history.house.gov/Institution/Election-Statistics/Election-Statistics/|publisher=[[Clerk of the United States House of Representatives|Clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives]]|date=February 28, 2019}}</ref> resigned on March 16, 2021, after she was confirmed to become the [[United States Secretary of the Interior|U.S. Secretary of the Interior]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 16, 2021 |title=Haaland officially bids farewell to U.S. House |work=[[Albuquerque Journal]] |url=https://www.abqjournal.com/2370258/haaland-delivers-farewell-address.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20210604062219/https://www.abqjournal.com/2370258/haaland-delivers-farewell-address.html |archive-date=June 4, 2021 |access-date=October 6, 2021 }}</ref> Democrat [[Melanie Stansbury]] won the June 1, 2021 [[2021 New Mexico's 1st congressional district special election|special election]] to finish her term with 60.4% of the vote.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gowins |first1=Max |title=Election Results: New Mexico 1st Congressional District Special Election |url=https://decisiondeskhq.com/election-results-new-mexico-1st-congressional-district-special-election/ |website=Decision Desk HQ |access-date=2021-06-15 |date=2021-06-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602004651/https://decisiondeskhq.com/election-results-new-mexico-1st-congressional-district-special-election/ |archive-date=June 2, 2021 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

{{see also|New Mexico's 2nd congressional district}}
The 2nd district encapsulates southern and western New Mexico, including the cities of [[Las Cruces, New Mexico|Las Cruces]], [[Carlsbad, New Mexico|Carlsbad]], and [[Alamogordo, New Mexico|Alamogordo]], as well as the southwestern suburbs of [[Albuquerque, New Mexico|Albuquerque]].<ref name="2023map" /> The incumbent was Republican [[Yvette Herrell]], who had flipped back the district from [[Xochitl Torres Small]] (who had in turn narrowly defeated her for the seat in a race to replace a Republican incumbent in 2018) with 53.7% of the vote in 2020.<ref name="clerk2020" /> The new 2022-2032 lines for the district made it more competitive for Democrats, with Vasquez defeating Herrell in a narrow race that was too close to call until the next afternoon.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Duerrmeyer |first=Tia |title=Democrats Make a Clean Sweep in New Mexico |work=Lea County Tribune |url=https://www.leacountytribune.com/2022/11/10/democratic-sweep/ |access-date=October 6, 2023 |archive-date=November 10, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221110165741/https://www.leacountytribune.com/2022/11/10/democratic-sweep/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

{{see also|New Mexico's 3rd congressional district}}
The 3rd district covers the northern and eastern parts of the state, taking in the cities of [[Santa Fe, New Mexico|Santa Fe]], [[Roswell, New Mexico|Roswell]], [[Farmington, New Mexico|Farmington]], and [[Clovis, New Mexico|Clovis]], as well as parts of the [[Navajo Nation]].<ref name="2023map" /> The incumbent was Democrat [[Teresa Leger Fernandez]], who was elected with 58.7% of the vote in 2020.<ref name="clerk2020" />
